section.title: Escalation, corroboration, and credible alternatives
section.deck: Ethan Evans explains why leaders can resist evidence of a weak manager and how careful, truthful framing can make a difficult career conversation easier to hear.

blocks.question: Have reports escalated problems with their managers to you, and why might a skip-level leader resist acting?
answer: Ethan Evans says such escalations were common. He describes an uncomfortable incentive: accepting one report’s account can create three problems for the skip-level leader—deciding what to do about the manager, replacing and training someone if necessary, and covering the work in between. Dismissing the report as oversensitive instead makes the problem easier to delegate back to the manager. Evans presents this as a possible subconscious bias, not a defense of ignoring a valid concern.

He recounts discovering a leader’s poor treatment of women only after several reports accumulated and he spoke with affected colleagues. A lone earlier report might not have moved him, a failure he describes candidly. Multiple independently supported accounts changed his understanding. He therefore recommends corroboration when colleagues are willing to provide it; the speaker’s “mutiny” metaphor concerns workplace escalation and should not obscure the seriousness of the example.
blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

followups.question: Should a high-performing IC compare observations with colleagues before escalating?
answer: If possible, yes. It first checks whether the problem is a broader pattern or a working-style mismatch. A colleague who works well with the manager may offer a useful adjustment; colleagues seeing the same problem may corroborate it. Shared dissatisfaction is not enough unless they are also willing to speak.

Evans proposes telling the skip-level leader that named colleagues are willing to share similar examples and asking the leader to speak with them. He thinks many leaders will do that, while explicitly refusing to guarantee it. The host flags the difference between casual complaints and formal escalation, including the possibility of retaliation or being wrong.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: Could you seek a move for business reasons instead of organizing an escalation?
answer: Evans separates two approaches. If there is a genuinely plausible case that another role would make the engineer equally or more valuable to the organization, lead with that case and do not introduce the manager complaint. If the real need is incompatible working relationships, explain that blame-free and think several moves ahead about the choices the leader actually has.

He describes his own move at Amazon. His leader wanted to keep him in the current role, but Evans had another available role outside that leader’s organization as well as a preferred role inside it. Explaining that remaining where he was had ceased to be an available choice changed the decision from “keep him here or move him internally” to “keep him in the organization or lose him.” After weeks of resistance, the internal move happened quickly. The story depends on having real alternatives, not on inventing an outside offer.
blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: How did you communicate those alternatives without sounding threatening?
answer: He framed the situation in terms the leader would recognize. Both were vice presidents, and the alternative offer came from a senior vice president. Evans explained that he needed to answer and that once he gave his word, he would have to honor it—as the leader himself would. That let the leader understand the constraint without a blunt demand.

Evans recommends preparing the key phrase before a predictable conversation rather than improvising under pressure. The facts and commitment should remain true; careful framing changes how the other person receives them. Delivery matters too. The same statement about needing to consider one’s career can sound hostile or calm and understandable depending on tone and body language.

He acknowledges that some engineers dislike workplace politics. His argument is that leaders still have emotions, stress, and defensiveness, so understanding the human interaction helps a person communicate an honest need more effectively. He does not claim he has fully figured out how to teach the skill.
blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

followups.question: Were there three different roles involved?
answer: Yes: the current role, the role he wanted inside the same organization, and another available role elsewhere. The host characterizes the alternative as leverage. Evans agrees with the underlying structure while emphasizing that he did not explicitly issue a threat; he stated the true consequence of accepting another offer and giving his word.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans
